chapter_theme: Remembering the absent lover as both the only thing keeping one alive and a burning pain. The chapter starts with a man's claim that memory itself gives joy, and turns to a woman who wonders whether she exists in his thoughts at all.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1201-1202 to the man, speaking to the friend who carried his message, and 1203-1210 to the woman. Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman.

1201.reading: The man says love is sweeter than liquor, because even thinking of it brings a great joy that doesn't fade.
1201.nuance: Parimelazhagar's headnote has him speaking to the friend who has carried his message: his claim is also a report of loneliness and faithfulness. The older comparison with liquor gains a new term here, since liquor needs drinking while love needs only memory.

1202.reading: Love is sweet in every way, since thinking of the beloved brings no pain; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man says how he has coped: love is sweet in union and in parting alike.
The woman rejects the friend's warning that her inability to endure will bring pain.
positions.quote: இது நீ இவ்வாறு ஆற்றாயாகின்றது துன்பம் பயக்குமென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் மறுத்துக் கூறியது.

1203.reading: The woman wonders if he seems about to think of her and doesn't, since a sneeze seems to come and then dies away.
1203.nuance: She reads her own body for evidence about his mind, using a folk belief that a sneeze means a distant loved one is thinking of you. Manakkudavar notes that she is repeating what ordinary women say, a rare moment of commentary on popular custom. An aborted sneeze makes for deflating, near-comic evidence.

1204.reading: The woman asks whether she too has a place in his heart, for, ah, he is always in hers.
1204.nuance: The verse uses the same indwelling that she argued for with such confidence in chapter 113, but now with doubt. Parimelazhagar extends the doubt into a tender either-or: is he kept away by unfinished work, or does he not remember her?

1205.reading: The woman asks whether he, who has barred her from his heart, isn't ashamed to keep coming into hers.
1205.nuance: Her thoughts of him are treated as his actions, so she can rebuke him for trespassing. கடிகொண்டார் means he has guarded his heart against her; Pope's prose, 'imprisoned me in his soul', gets this backwards, though his couplet has it right.

1206.reading: The woman asks what else she could live by, since she lives only by remembering the days she shared with him.
1206.nuance: Parimelazhagar sets it as a reply to the friend's advice to forget. He lists the things she lacks that would otherwise sustain her: his messenger, sending her own. Memory is what is left.

1207.reading: The woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she doesn't know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
1207.nuance: A precise bind: remembering burns her, and forgetting would kill her, as Parimelazhagar supplies. Compare 1206, where memory is what keeps her alive.

1208.reading: The woman says that however much she thinks of him, he doesn't get angry; that much is the honour her lover does her.
1208.nuance: All she can claim is that he doesn't object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar hears the sarcasm directed at her friend's promise that he will come and bring her joy. Manakkudavar defines grace as not getting angry even at a fault, so the 'honour' is very small.

1209.reading: The woman says her dear life is ending, as she thinks too much about the lack of grace in one who said they weren't separate.
1209.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a key distinction: in her own words, it's not the parting that is killing her, but his lack of love.

1210.reading: The woman speaks to the moon, blessing it and asking about seeing with her eyes the man who went away without leaving her.
1210.nuance: விடாஅது சென்றாரை, 'who left without leaving', packs the whole chapter's paradox into two words.

positions.position: She begs the moon not to set, so that their eyes can meet on it while both look at it.
positions.quote: மதி இருவரானும் நோக்கப்படுதலின் இருவர் கண்ணும் அதன்கண்ணே சேர்தல்.

positions.position: She reproaches the moon for not setting: if it set she could sleep and see him in dreams.
positions.quote: பட்டதாயின், என் கண் உறங்கும்; உறங்கினால், அவரைக் காணலாமென் பது கருத்து.

positions.position: She asks it not to set, to give her light to seek him out with her eyes.
positions.quote: நான் என் கண்களால் தேடிக் கண்டுபிடித்திடத் துணையாக நீ மறையாமல் இருப்பாயாக.

links.note: 1202 says thinking of the beloved brings no pain, and 1207 says even thinking burns. If Parimelazhagar is right that a man speaks 1202 and a woman 1207, then the chapter makes a pointed contrast between their experience of memory.
1122 is the man's oath: the bond is like body and life. 1209 quotes the same promise, வேறல்லம், as the thing killing her. In 1124 he had said her going was death to him, and now she is the one dying.

In 1119, the man tells the moon not to appear, as no one else should have her beauty. In 1210, the woman begs the moon to stay, since it's the only thing she may share with him. His moon is a rival to exclusive possession, and hers is the only link she has.
1090 says love beats liquor because sight alone is enough. 1201 says memory alone is enough. As he moves away, the comparison holds, and needs less and less of her presence.

source_issues: 1201: Manakkudavar's entry has நாமம் where the verse has காமம், a typo.
1202: The verse text has எனைத்தொனறு ஏனிதேகாண் where other sources read எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண், apparently corrupt.
1204: Parimelazhagar's entry starts with the fragment தோஒ வுளரே யவர், the end of the verse text.
1205: Parimelazhagar's gloss ends with என்றான், the masculine form, for a verse spoken by the woman, apparently a typo; Manakkudavar's entry has several garbled words, such as எர்மை and காணாபோ.
1210: Parimelazhagar reports a variant, படாது, that yields the reading Manakkudavar gives.
